evidence_quotes.quote: They argued that there were social objectives to be achieved in informal settlements, notably access to clean water, which should override maximizing revenue as the principal goal for the water company.

Illegal connections could be regularized. Unpaid water bills could be resolved, with large disputed bills (which had arisen before the devolution of the water company, at a time, the MBK chairman said, when there was wide corruption) waived and real bills paid in instalments.
They did not check if a connection was legal or illegal. We have a meter and an agreement to pay accumulated bills, legalize. Here, they went to the main and disconnected pipes
Water is the economic base, the chairman has the authority to decide the number of people he wants to have connections.

It is based on interviews with households, water company ofﬁcials and former ofﬁcials, water vendors and landlords and on the experience of the second author working and living in Kibera for three years.
The average of water actually stored when the women were interviewed around midday was 76 litres which represents 11 lcd, a tiny proportion of internationally estimated basic needs of 25–50 lcd.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and settlement-level drinking and domestic water service access in Nairobi informal settlements (Kibera, Mukuru and Mathare).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines municipal utility devolution under Kenya's 2002 Water Act, informal-settlement governance initiatives, vendor associations and community participation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) law-enforcement and utility mass disconnections of illegal and legal pipe connections in Mathare and Kibera (enforcement and administrative reconnection requirements); (2) negotiated regularization of illicit connections, waiver of disputed arrears and instalment billing rules with Maji Bora Kibera (accommodation and cost-recovery/billing rules); and (3) utility regulatory/delegated governance structure and connection-allocation discretion under the delegated meter chamber model in Mukuru and Mathare, where chamber chairmen held delegated authority over who received connections and cartels captured and resold connections at monopoly prices, alongside the Informal Settlements Unit policy mandate prioritizing access over revenue maximization.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal and institutional empirical case study drawing on primary interviews in 2008 and 2010 with women from 14 Kibera households, Nairobi Water Company officials and sociologists, former officials, water vendors and landlords, utility socio-economic appraisal data on 16 meter chambers in Mukuru, and three years of field experience in Kibera. Qualitative empirical studies are eligible for systematic review inclusion and mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service-access outcomes across household and settlement units of analysis: pipe connection and mass disconnection (including a week-long total cut-off in Mathare followed by emergency free standpipes), monopoly capture of meter-chamber connections and connection resale prices in Mukuru, household water availability and rationing, per-capita stored/collected water quantities (lcd), water prices and expenditure share of income, queuing/collection time, and curtailed household activities.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (households/women, water vendors and informal settlements — Kibera, Mukuru and Mathare — in Nairobi, Kenya), exposures (utility devolution and Informal Settlements Unit policy, vendor connection regularization/billing agreements, police-backed mass disconnections, and delegated meter-chamber governance arrangements), outcomes (connections/disconnections, availability, quantity, collection time and affordability/prices), and study design (qualitative empirical case study) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (semi-structured/key-informant interviews with households, vendors, landlords and utility officials, utility appraisal records and field observation)
population_and_sample: Informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya (primarily Kibera, plus Mukuru and Mathare); qualitative primary interviews with women from 14 Kibera households (8 Makina Women's Group members and 6 SODIS-user households), Nairobi Water Company officials/sociologists and former officials, water vendors (including Maji Bora Kibera leadership) and landlords, plus utility appraisal of account holders across 16 meter chambers in Mukuru.
exposure: Municipal utility devolution (2002 Water Act creating Nairobi Water and Sewerage Company and its Informal Settlements Unit shifting priority from revenue maximization to access), negotiated regularization of illegal connections and bill-waiver/instalment arrangements with Maji Bora Kibera, police-backed enforcement mass disconnections of legal and illegal water pipes, and delegated meter-chamber regulatory/subcontracting arrangements governing connection allocation and billing in Mukuru and Mathare.
outcome: Household and settlement water access, pipe connection and mass disconnection, cartel capture and resale pricing of meter-chamber connections, water supply continuity/rationing, household water expenditure and vendor jerry-can prices, water collection time, stored/collected water quantity (litres per capita per day), and deferred household hygiene/cooking tasks.
rationale: Full-text qualitative socio-legal and institutional empirical study examining water service access in Nairobi informal settlements (Kibera, Mukuru and Mathare). It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism scope of Criterion 2 by empirically investigating enforcement via police/utility indiscriminate mass disconnections and office reconnection procedures, negotiated regularization of illegal connections and arrears waivers/instalments, utility organizational/cost-recovery mandates for informal settlements, and delegated meter-chamber connection-allocation discretion and monopoly capture. Qualitative empirical evidence is fully eligible for systematic-review mechanism synthesis.
